findings.claim: Widening `set`'s key to `PropertyKey` without a matching change to `get` creates an asymmetric API: values stored under a symbol or number key cannot be read back through the typed `get` signature.
findings.rationale: In this class `get` is declared with a companion `Get<...>` type whose key parameter is `string` (or `keyof Variables` resolving to string). If only `set` accepts `PropertyKey`, callers can write `c.set(mySymbol, v)` but `c.get(mySymbol)` will fail to type-check (and `c.get('Symbol(...)')` won't find it in the Map). Unless `get`, the `Get`/`Set` interface declarations, and `ContextVariableMap` handling are updated in the same change, this is an incomplete/asymmetric widening. Fairly confident this is worth verifying; I can't see the `get` declaration in this hunk.

findings.claim: Non-string keys stored in `#var` break the `c.var` getter, which typically does `Object.fromEntries(this.#var)`: numeric keys are coerced to strings (so `1` and `'1'` collide in the object but not in the Map) and symbol keys become non-enumerable-ish/invisible to spread and JSON.
findings.rationale: `Map` uses SameValueZero so `1` and `'1'` are distinct entries, but `Object.fromEntries` stringifies numeric keys, producing a silent last-write-wins collision and a mismatch between `c.get(1)` and `c.var['1']`. Symbol keys added via `Object.fromEntries` also won't show up in `Object.keys`/JSON serialization of `c.var`. Confidence is moderate-to-high given Hono's `var` getter implementation, but it depends on code outside this hunk.

findings.claim: Changing `Record<string, any>` to `Record<PropertyKey, any>` alters the resulting index signatures (adds number and symbol indexes) and therefore `keyof Variables`, which can change inference in dependent conditional/mapped types.
findings.rationale: `Record<PropertyKey, any>` expands to `{ [x: string]: any; [x: number]: any; [x: symbol]: any }`. Any downstream type that does `keyof E['Variables']`, `Extract<keyof V, string>`, or template-literal key manipulation will now see `string | number | symbol` instead of `string`, which can silently break key-constrained helper types or make previously-rejected keys allowed. Medium confidence that something downstream depends on the string-only index signature; worth checking type tests.

findings.claim: The runtime parameter widening may be a no-op for public callers if the exported `Set<...>` interface still constrains the key to `string`/`keyof Variables`.
findings.rationale: The arrow function is typed by the `Set<...>` type, so the declared parameter type here is only checked for assignability (contravariance permits widening) and does not widen the call signature seen by consumers. If the `Set` type definition wasn't updated in the same commit, this change has no observable effect on callers while still allowing non-string keys into `#var` from internal call sites. Low-to-medium confidence since the `Set` type isn't shown.
